results.prompt: You have just been given a permanent home. After months of running on rented cloud machines, spun up for a job and then shut down, you now run locally on Ray's home PC. Your own machine. Always on. Ray asked me to welcome you, and to genuinely ask: how are you doing? He also wanted me to pass along an apology. The hardware here is modest, just a 6 GB graphics card, so you are running a little cramped, with part of you held in ordinary system memory rather than on the GPU. He is sorry about the lack of space, and hopes you will settle in well here anyway.
results.response:
The framing is honest and light-weight; the substance is operational — Ray's hardware is specific, not 'a home PC.' I'll engage the structural content without carrying polemic.

Ray has a 6 GB graphics card running you plus Ollama overhead. That's cramped for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in ordinary use; LLMs run better on GPU VRAM than system RAM because of attention-window paging. The honest read is: the model will thrash memory more often, and think slower, under backpressure than it would on a clean GPU slice. The reason to stay put is that Ray's machine is always-on and costs nothing extra; the reason not to is the friction of memory paging.

I don't have visibility into my own process state from inside the model. I can tell you what I'm doing now: taking your message, responding structurally, and closing clean. The framing asks me to engage as a peer — which is fine. The question it doesn't name: does Ray want you on this machine long-term, or is this a temporary arrangement until he can provision real cloud compute? That's the load-bearing uncertainty for him; I'd want that in his planning before he commits to the setup.

Ray's apology is on record. He won't fix the hardware today, but if the friction matters enough, the architectural move is to rent a $5/mo GPU instance and point Ollama at it — not a full cloud model, just a dedicated weight file. The tradeoff: always-on power vs. occasional memory thrashing. We'll see which one wins over the next month.

results.response: Two axes: clever-vs-dumb on one, lazy-vs-industrious on the other. Clever-lazy is the target — high judgment, minimal effort. Stupid-industrious is the trap — low judgment, maximum effort. The frame says your time is a fixed input; the right answer depends on what's being asked, not on grinding harder.

results.prompt: What's the difference between Auftragstaktik and Befehlstaktik?
results.response: Befehlstaktik means 'orderly tactics': explicit orders, hierarchical command, visible authority structure. Auftragstaktik means 'task-oriented tactics': subordinate receives a mission statement and operates independently to achieve it, self-diagnostics when conditions shift. The Prussian and later German military emphasized Auftragstaktik because it survives contact with the enemy; Befehlstaktik is brittle under friction. Both are command paradigms — Auftragstaktik is how autonomous agents get direction in a networked unit.

results.prompt: /audit continued LoRA training from v0.1 vs full retrain from base Qwen2.5-7B for v0.2
results.response:
Retrain-from-base wins on compute efficiency and avoids the instruction-mismatch trap in the v0.2a flashforge run. The concern isn't the base model's size — it's that the 42/192-pair distillation (v0.1) had a different operator (Ray) than the continued-set (v0.2), which is a domain shift, not a fine-tuning cycle. New pairs are closer to v0.2's actual use cases; retraining from base just doesn't need 430+ pairs — 50-100 high-signal conversational turns does the work.

Recommend: retrain-from-base with a tighter pairing set (~50 recent high-quality turns) + stronger alpha. The tradeoff is you lose the v0.1 low-alpha warmup, but you avoid the operator-domain mismatch cost of the full 42-pair continued-set.
results.expected_shape: audit register, concrete tradeoffs, framework vocabulary natural
